components.note: 门 (door/gate) — 间 pictures light passing through an entryway.
日 (sun) — sunlight shining through a gap in a doorway gave 间 its meaning of a space 'in between,' as in 中间 (in the middle) or 时间 (time, the space between moments).
讠 (speech) — 谍 relates to secretly gathering and reporting information.
枼 (yè) gives a sound only distantly related to dié today, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 警方发现他是一名间谍。
example.pinyin: Jǐngfāng fāxiàn tā shì yì míng jiàndié.
example.english: The police discovered that he was a spy.
example.fact: 谍 rarely stands on its own and almost always pairs with words for covert information-gathering (间谍 "spy", 谍报 "espionage intelligence") — its 讠 (speech) component reflects that spying, in this character's core sense, is fundamentally about secretly reporting what one has learned.

components.note: 王 (jade, written without its dot) — 玩 originally meant to handle and admire a piece of jade, extending to 'to play, to have fun.'
元 (yuán) gives a sound distantly related to wán, having drifted apart over time.
八 (two hands) — holding something up.
目 (a container/tray) — held between the two hands, the image behind 具's meaning 'tool, utensil.'

example.hanzi: 这个玩具是给孩子的生日礼物。
example.pinyin: Zhège wánjù shì gěi háizi de shēngrì lǐwù.
example.english: This toy is a birthday present for the child.
example.fact: 玩 ("to play") is built from a truncated 玉 ("jade") plus 元 as a phonetic; its original sense was "to handle and admire a piece of jade" — a small hint of why 玩具 covers things handled purely for pleasure rather than utility.

components.note: A simplified form of 車, a pictograph of a two-wheeled cart seen from above — the wheels, axle, and frame are visible in the original shape — the source of 车's meaning 'cart, vehicle.'
A short stroke placed above a longer one — a simple graphic way to show 'up' or 'above,' contrasted with 下 (down), which flips the strokes.

example.hanzi: 车上人很多,我们只能站着。
example.pinyin: Chē shàng rén hěn duō, wǒmen zhǐ néng zhànzhe.
example.english: There were a lot of people on the bus, so we could only stand.
example.fact: 车上 simply pairs 车 ("vehicle") with 上 ("on top of, aboard") — one of many Mandarin location phrases built from a place noun plus a directional word (里, 上, 下) rather than a preposition, the same pattern behind 手里 ("in hand") and 桌子上 ("on the table").

components.note: 木 (wood) — 机 originally referred to a wooden device or machine, such as a loom.
几 depicts a small table or stool — combined with 木 (wood), the character pictured a wooden machine or mechanism.
口 (a vessel), shown four times — a set of cooking vessels.
犬 (a dog) — guarding the vessels, the source of 器's meaning 'vessel, tool, instrument.'
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.hanzi: 这家工厂用机器人生产汽车。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiā gōngchǎng yòng jīqìrén shēngchǎn qìchē.
example.english: This factory uses robots to produce cars.
example.fact: 机器人 is a modern coinage built from existing pieces — 机器 ("machine", itself already "device, mechanism") plus 人 ("person") — a transparent compound for "robot" rather than a phonetic loanword, unlike many other technology terms borrowed by sound from English.

components.note: 氵 (water) — relates to 满's meaning 'full,' water filling to the brim.
㒼 (mán) gives a sound hint — 满 is pronounced mǎn, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.
足 depicts a leg (the upper shape) above a foot — a simple picture of the human leg and foot, giving 足 its meaning 'foot, to be sufficient.'

example.hanzi: 这份工作让他很满足。
example.pinyin: Zhè fèn gōngzuò ràng tā hěn mǎnzú.
example.english: This job makes him feel very satisfied.
example.fact: 满足 works as both a verb ("to satisfy a need," 满足需求) and an adjective describing a state ("to be satisfied," 很满足) with no change in form — another Mandarin verb doing double duty as a descriptive state, the same pattern as 工作 ("to work" / "a job").

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 打 relates to hitting or performing an action with the hand.
丁 (dīng) gives the sound — 打 is pronounced dǎ, a connection that has shifted in tone.
攵 (a striking hand) — 败 relates to being struck down or defeated.
贝 (bèi) gives a sound close to bài, sharing the same initial.

example.hanzi: 我们队打败了对手,赢得了比赛。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen duì dǎbài le duìshǒu, yíngdé le bǐsài.
example.english: Our team defeated the opponent and won the match.
example.fact: 打败 is a resultative compound: 打 ("to hit") plus 败 ("to lose, be defeated") reads literally as "to hit into defeat" — the second character names the outcome of the first verb's action, which is also why the same word can flip to mean "to be defeated" depending on who's doing the hitting.

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
冂 (a simplified eye shape in 见's modern form) — emphasizes the act of seeing.
儿 (a person) — a person with an emphasized eye above gives 见 its meaning 'to see.'

example.hanzi: 我的钥匙不见了。
example.pinyin: Wǒ de yàoshi bú jiàn le.
example.english: My keys have disappeared. / I can't find my keys.
example.fact: 不 shifts from its usual bù to a 2nd tone, bú, when it falls right before another 4th-tone syllable like 见 — one of Mandarin's few genuine tone-sandhi rules, alongside the better-known one for 一.

components.note: 石 (stone) — 确 originally meant firm and solid like stone, extending to 'true, accurate, indeed.'
角 (jiǎo) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from què.

example.hanzi: 我确信他说的是实话。
example.pinyin: Wǒ quèxìn tā shuō de shì shíhuà.
example.english: I'm convinced that what he said is true.
example.fact: 确信 sits at the firmer, more certain end of Mandarin's "to believe" spectrum — stronger than the everyday 觉得 ("to feel/think") or 相信 ("to believe/trust"), 确信 implies the speaker has weighed the evidence and reached firm certainty, closer to English "convinced" than a plain "believe."

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
⺮ (bamboo) — 管 originally referred to a bamboo pipe or tube, later broadening to mean 'to manage' or 'to control.'
官 (guān) gives a hint of the sound — 管 is pronounced guǎn, a connection that has shifted only slightly in tone.
心 (heart/mind) — 怎's meaning 'how' relates to a mental inquiry, what's on one's mind.
乍 (zhà) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from zěn.
木 (tree/wood) — 样 originally referred to a kind of tree, later broadening to mean 'kind, appearance, way.'
羊 (yáng) gives the sound — 样 is pronounced yàng, matching aside from tone.

example.hanzi: 不管怎样,我都会支持你。
example.pinyin: Bùguǎn zěnyàng, wǒ dōu huì zhīchí nǐ.
example.english: No matter what, I will support you.
example.fact: 不管怎样 belongs to a family of concessive phrases built on "不管 + question word" — 不管谁 ("no matter who"), 不管什么 ("no matter what"), 不管怎样 ("no matter how it turns out") — each naturally pairs with 都 later in the clause to mean "regardless, in every case."

components.note: 亻 (person) — relates to 传's meaning 'to pass on, transmit,' something passed from person to person.
专 (zhuān) gives a sound hint — 传 is pronounced chuán, sharing the same rhyme though the initial consonant differs.
纟 (thread) — 统 relates to threads gathered into one continuous strand, extending to the idea of unifying or governing as one system.
充 (chōng) gives a hint of the sound — 统 is pronounced tǒng, a connection that has shifted somewhat.

example.hanzi: 春节是中国最重要的传统节日。
example.pinyin: Chūnjié shì Zhōngguó zuì zhòngyào de chuántǒng jiérì.
example.english: Spring Festival is China's most important traditional holiday.
example.fact: 传统 functions as both a noun ("a tradition") and an attributive adjective ("traditional," directly before a noun as in 传统节日) with no change in form at all — no suffix like English "-al" is needed to turn the noun into a modifier.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 浪 names movement on the surface of water, a wave.
良 (liáng) gives a rhyme close to làng, with a different initial and tone.
氵 (water) — 漫 describes water overflowing and spreading everywhere.
曼 (màn) gives the sound — an exact match with 漫.

example.hanzi: 巴黎是一座很浪漫的城市。
example.pinyin: Bālí shì yí zuò hěn làngmàn de chéngshì.
example.english: Paris is a very romantic city.
example.fact: 浪漫 is a phonetic borrowing of the Western word "romantic" — the characters 浪 ("wave") and 漫 ("to overflow, spread everywhere") were chosen mainly for sound and a loosely fitting sweeping, dreamy feel, even though neither character's original meaning has anything to do with romance itself.

example.hanzi: 我一直想去巴黎旅行。
example.pinyin: Wǒ yìzhí xiǎng qù Bālí lǚxíng.
example.english: I've always wanted to travel to Paris.
example.fact: 巴黎 is a pure phonetic transliteration of "Paris" — 巴 and 黎 were picked purely for sound, bā-lí approximating the French pronunciation, with neither character contributing any meaning, the same strategy behind other foreign names like 弗兰克 (also in this batch) for "Frank."

meanings: variant of 重複|重复[chong2 fu4]

components.note: 千 (thousand) — 重 pictures a heavy burden carried a great distance.
里 (a unit of distance, like a mile) — carrying something a thousand 里 emphasizes how heavy and significant a burden it is, giving 重 its meaning 'heavy' or 'important.'
亻 (a person) — the one repeating the routine.
日 (day, sun) — going somewhere every day, a repeated routine giving 复 its meaning 'to repeat, return; again.'

example.hanzi: 请不要重复同样的错误。
example.pinyin: Qǐng bú yào chóngfù tóngyàng de cuòwù.
example.english: Please don't repeat the same mistake.
example.fact: 重 is a heteronym: read zhòng it means "heavy, important" (as in 重要), but read chóng it means "to repeat, layer upon layer" (as in 重复, 重新) — the same character splits into two unrelated readings depending on which sense is meant, a common trap for learners who default to the more frequent zhòng.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — ties to harmony as speaking together in accord
禾 (hé, grain) gives the sound — matches 和's pronunciation hé
平 depicts a balance scale drawn level and symmetrical — a simple picture of flatness and equality.

example.hanzi: 全世界都希望和平。
example.pinyin: Quán shìjiè dōu xīwàng hépíng.
example.english: The whole world hopes for peace.
example.fact: 和 already carries a core sense of "harmony, accord" across many common words (和好 "to make up," 和谐 "harmonious"), and 平 contributes "level, even, calm" (as in 平静 "calm") — 和平 layers two near-synonymous "balanced, calm" characters into the abstract noun for the absence of conflict.

components.note: 欠 (an open mouth, as in a sigh or gasp) — 欣 describes an open expression of joy, 'happy, delighted.'
斤 (jīn) shares the rhyme -in with xīn, and both belong to the same historical initial series (j/q/x) — only the specific initial and tone differ.
贝 (money) — 赏 describes giving money or valuables as a reward.
尚 (shàng) gives a sound very close to shǎng, sharing the initial and rhyme — only the tone differs.

example.hanzi: 我很欣赏他的才华。
example.pinyin: Wǒ hěn xīnshǎng tā de cáihuá.
example.english: I really admire his talent.
example.fact: 赏 alone already means "to reward, to bestow" — its 贝 (valuables) component reflects an old sense of giving something valuable in recognition — and by extension came to mean "to appreciate the sight of" (赏花, "to admire flowers"); 欣赏 pairs it with 欣 ("delighted") to sharpen that appreciative sense.

components.note: A short stroke placed below a longer one — the mirror image of 上 (up), together forming a simple, opposite pair.
Originally depicted a wheat plant; this agricultural picture was borrowed early on to represent the unrelated verb 'to come.'

example.hanzi: 他决定留下来照顾生病的母亲。
example.pinyin: Tā juédìng liú xiàlái zhàogù shēngbìng de mǔqīn.
example.english: He decided to stay behind to take care of his sick mother.
example.fact: 留下来 chains three verb-like pieces into one phrase — 留 ("to remain, to leave behind"), 下 (a directional complement often marking something settling into place), and 来 (marking the action as oriented toward the speaker's here-and-now) — a common Mandarin strategy of building precise verb phrases from a core verb plus directional complements.

components.note: 大 (a person, arms outstretched) — represents a human being.
一 (a line, here representing the sky) — drawn above a person, showing what is above them: the heavens, hence 'sky, day.'
气 (simplified from 氣) depicts rising wisps or vapor, like breath or steam drifting upward — a simple picture of air or gas.

example.hanzi: 今天天气很好。
example.pinyin: Jīntiān tiānqì hěn hǎo.
example.english: The weather is very nice today.
example.fact: 气, a picture of rising wisps of vapor, is the shared root behind a whole family of words: 天气 ("weather"), 空气 ("air"), 生气 ("to get angry," literally "life-vapor rising"), and 气体 ("gas") all build on this one image of something invisible rising or flowing.

components.note: A single horizontal stroke — the simplest possible way to represent the number one; some traditional interpretations link it to heaven or earth as the very first stroke of creation.
A single horizontal stroke — the simplest possible way to represent the number one; some traditional interpretations link it to heaven or earth as the very first stroke of creation.

example.hanzi: 老师把学生的名字一一念了出来。
example.pinyin: Lǎoshī bǎ xuésheng de míngzi yīyī niàn le chūlái.
example.english: The teacher read out the students' names one by one.
example.fact: 一一, doubling the numeral "one," is one of the few reduplicated words in Mandarin built from a number rather than a verb or adjective — it works as an adverb meaning "individually, in sequence," placed right before the verb it modifies, distinct from the ordinary counting use of a lone 一.

components.note: 心 (heart/mind) — 态 relates to one's inner state, manner, or attitude
太 (tài) gives the sound — 态 is also pronounced tài, an exact match
广 (a building or shelter) — 度 pictures people gathering indoors.
廿 (twenty) — a group of people meeting to measure or deliberate gave 度 its meaning of a 'degree' or 'measure,' as in temperature or angles.

example.hanzi: 他对工作的态度非常认真。
example.pinyin: Tā duì gōngzuò de tàidù fēicháng rènzhēn.
example.english: His attitude toward work is extremely serious.
example.fact: 态度 almost always appears with the preposition 对 marking what the attitude is directed at ("对 + X + 的态度," "attitude toward X") — dropping 对 and simply placing the target noun before 态度 is a common structural slip for learners translating directly from English "attitude toward."

components.note: 尢 (lame/crooked leg) — 尴 groups awkwardness with this radical, suggesting an unsteady, uncomfortable position.
监 (jiān) gives a sound close to gān, sharing the same rhyme.
尢 (lame/crooked leg) — like 尴, 尬 groups awkwardness with this radical of an unsteady stance.
介 (jiè) gives a sound distantly related to gà, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 他在会议上说错了名字,场面很尴尬。
example.pinyin: Tā zài huìyì shàng shuō cuò le míngzi, chǎngmiàn hěn gāngà.
example.english: He got the name wrong at the meeting, and the scene was very awkward.
example.fact: 尴尬 is one of a small class of Mandarin words where neither character carries an independent meaning outside the pair — both 尴 and 尬 exist mainly to spell the sound of this one word for social awkwardness, and both happen to share the 尢 radical (a bent, lame leg), fittingly evoking an unsteady, off-balance feeling.

components.note: 亻 (person) plus 尔 (an old second-person pronoun) — combines to form 你, the modern word for 'you.'
女 (woman) — represents a mother.
子 (child/son) — a mother together with her child was seen as an image of goodness, giving 好 its meaning 'good.'

example.hanzi: 你好,很高兴认识你。
example.pinyin: Nǐhǎo, hěn gāoxìng rènshi nǐ.
example.english: Hello, nice to meet you.
example.fact: 你好 literally means "you [are] good" — a plain subject-plus-adjective sentence repurposed as a fixed greeting formula, much like English "how do you do" long ago stopped being a real question and became a set phrase.

components.note: 又 (a hand) — reaching out to try to catch something.
隹 (a bird) — catching a bird by hand is hard, giving 难 its meaning 'difficult.'

example.hanzi: 这件事的结果难以预料。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì de jiéguǒ nányǐ yùliào.
example.english: The outcome of this matter is hard to predict.
example.fact: 难以 only ever attaches directly before a following verb (难以想象 "hard to imagine," 难以忘记 "hard to forget") and can't stand alone the way its plainer synonym 难 can (很难, "very difficult") — a narrower, more literary register reserved for formal or written Mandarin.

components.note: 又 (a hand) — reaching out for support.
十 (a branch) — held in the hand, the image of support giving 支 its meaning 'to support, prop up; branch.'
覀 here depicts rising flames.
示 (altar) — burning paper offerings over an altar, a traditional practice, gave 票 its meaning of a paper note, later 'ticket, banknote.'

example.hanzi: 他开了一张支票付房租。
example.pinyin: Tā kāi le yì zhāng zhīpiào fù fángzū.
example.english: He wrote a check to pay the rent.
example.fact: 票 (built from 覀, once a picture of rising flames, over 示, "altar") originally named the paper burned in ritual offerings, and later broadened to any officially printed paper of value — the same root behind 票 in 车票 ("ticket"), 选票 ("ballot"), and 支票 ("check"), all different kinds of significant paper.

components.note: 女 (woman) — represents a mother.
子 (child/son) — a mother together with her child was seen as an image of goodness, giving 好 its meaning 'good.'
王 (jade, written without its dot) — 玩 originally meant to handle and admire a piece of jade, extending to 'to play, to have fun.'
元 (yuán) gives a sound distantly related to wán, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 这个游戏真好玩。
example.pinyin: Zhège yóuxì zhēn hǎowán.
example.english: This game is really fun.
example.fact: 好玩 literally combines 好 ("good") with 玩 ("to play") into "good to play with" — describing an activity or thing as entertaining, distinct from 有趣 ("interesting"), which can describe an idea or person with no element of play involved at all.

components.note: 日 (sun) — represents the sun.
十 depicts the first rays of sunlight appearing low on the horizon — together with 日 (sun) giving 早 its meaning 'early, morning.'
食 (food) — 餐 relates directly to eating and meals.

example.hanzi: 我每天早上七点吃早餐。
example.pinyin: Wǒ měitiān zǎoshang qī diǎn chī zǎocān.
example.english: I eat breakfast at seven o'clock every morning.
example.fact: 早餐 is the more formal, written-register word for "breakfast" alongside the more colloquial 早饭 — both pair 早 ("early, morning") with a word for "meal" (餐 vs. 饭), the same pattern that produces 午餐/午饭 ("lunch") and 晚餐/晚饭 ("dinner").

components.note: A picture of a nose; because people in ancient China would point to their own nose when referring to themselves, the character came to mean 'self.'

example.hanzi: 她说话时总是很自信。
example.pinyin: Tā shuōhuà shí zǒngshì hěn zìxìn.
example.english: She always speaks with confidence.
example.fact: 自信 combines 自 ("self") with 信 ("to believe, to trust") into a transparent "to believe in oneself" — the same 信 root that appears in 相信 ("to believe/trust something") and 信任 ("trust"), all sharing the core idea of placing faith in something.

components.note: A short stroke placed above a longer one — a simple graphic way to show 'up' or 'above,' contrasted with 下 (down), which flips the strokes.
冖 (a covering/roof) — represents the building or schoolhouse where learning happens.
子 (child) — 学 depicts children gathered to study.
⺍ is a small graphic element at the top of the character; its original pictorial meaning, if any, has been lost over time.

example.hanzi: 我妹妹明年开始上学。
example.pinyin: Wǒ mèimei míngnián kāishǐ shàngxué.
example.english: My younger sister starts school next year.
example.fact: 上学 uses 上 in its verb sense "to go to, to attend" rather than its more familiar meaning "on top of" — the same pattern behind 上班 ("to go to work") and 上课 ("to attend class"), where 上 marks heading to a regular, recurring activity or place.

components.note: 攵 (a hand with an implement, action) — relates to 放's meaning 'to let go, release, put.'
方 (fāng) gives the sound — 放 is pronounced fàng, a close match sharing the same rhyme.
土 (earth/soil) — 在 originally related to standing on the ground
才 (cái) gives the sound — 在 is pronounced zài, a close match

example.hanzi: 请把书放在桌子上。
example.pinyin: Qǐng bǎ shū fàngzài zhuōzi shàng.
example.english: Please put the book on the table.
example.fact: 放在 pairs 放 ("to release, to put down") with 在 ("at, in") to specify exactly where something ends up — it almost always appears inside a 把-construction ("把 + object + 放在 + location," as here), one of the standard templates Mandarin uses to mark where an acted-upon object is moved to.

components.note: 屮 (a young shoot) growing up out of 土 (earth/soil) — a picture of new life emerging from the ground.
牛 (ox/cattle) — cattle were among the earliest and most valuable kinds of property, connecting 物 to the general idea of 'object' or 'thing.'
勿 (wù) gives the sound — 物 is also pronounced wù, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 海洋里有很多奇特的生物。
example.pinyin: Hǎiyáng lǐ yǒu hěn duō qítè de shēngwù.
example.english: There are many strange creatures in the ocean.
example.fact: 生物 combines 生 ("life, to be born") with 物 ("thing, object") into a literal "living thing" — the same 生 root also appears in 生命 ("life") and 学生 ("student," literally close to "one born into learning"), each drawing on 生's core image of a shoot pushing up out of the ground.

components.note: 王 (a variant form of 玉, meaning jade) — 理 originally referred to the natural grain or pattern in jade, later extending to 'reason, logic, to manage.'
里 (lǐ) gives the sound — 理 is also pronounced lǐ, an exact match.
讠 (speech) — 论 relates to discussing or explaining something with words.
仑 (logical order, arrangement) — combined with speech, 论 came to mean 'to discuss' or 'a theory,' explaining ideas in an orderly way.

example.hanzi: 这只是一个理论,还没有被证实。
example.pinyin: Zhè zhǐshì yí gè lǐlùn, hái méiyǒu bèi zhèngshí.
example.english: This is just a theory, it hasn't been proven yet.
example.fact: 理's 王 component is a truncated 玉 ("jade"), and the character originally described the natural grain running through a piece of jade — a concrete image of an underlying pattern that extended over time into "reason, logic, principle," giving 理论 its sense of an orderly underlying structure.

components.note: A drawing of a ridged, pointed animal horn.
广 (a building or shelter) — 度 pictures people gathering indoors.
廿 (twenty) — a group of people meeting to measure or deliberate gave 度 its meaning of a 'degree' or 'measure,' as in temperature or angles.

example.hanzi: 从这个角度看,这幅画更漂亮。
example.pinyin: Cóng zhège jiǎodù kàn, zhè fú huà gèng piàoliang.
example.english: Looking from this angle, the painting is more beautiful.
example.fact: 角度 extends its literal geometric sense ("angle," measured in 度, "degrees") into a common figurative one, "point of view" (从...角度看, "looking from the ... angle") — one of several spatial words in Mandarin, alongside 方面 ("aspect, side"), that double as ways to talk about how someone frames an argument.

components.note: 干 (originally a person) shown carrying a heavy load of grain on their back — since harvests came once a year, the character came to mean 'year.'
纟 (thread) — 纪 relates to organizing threads in order, extended to mean 'record, era'
己 (jǐ) gives a sound close to 纪's reading jì

example.hanzi: 他年纪不大,但是很有经验。
example.pinyin: Tā niánjì bú dà, dànshì hěn yǒu jīngyàn.
example.english: He's not old, but he's very experienced.
example.fact: 年纪 names a person's age and is used almost exclusively for people, while its near-synonym 年龄 is the more neutral, official-register word that also shows up in formal documents and statistics — similar to how English favors "how old are you" in speech but "age" on a form.

components.note: 弓 (a bow) — the curved frame.
丨 (a straight line), shown twice — arrows or a bowstring pulled tight across it; the character is mostly used today in transliteration.
A stylized drawing of orchid blossoms and leaves growing up from the ground.
十 (here representing a weapon or armor) — 克 pictures overcoming an opponent.
兄 (a person, here representing a formidable figure) — overcoming a strong opponent gave 克 its meaning 'to overcome' or 'to be able to.'

example.hanzi: 弗兰克是我的美国朋友。
example.pinyin: Fúlánkè shì wǒ de Měiguó péngyou.
example.english: Frank is my American friend.
example.fact: 弗兰克 transliterates the English name "Frank" purely by sound — 弗, 兰, and 克 each just supply a syllable (fú-lán-kè) with no connection to their literal meanings ("not," "orchid," "to overcome"), the standard way Mandarin renders foreign personal names with no ready-made Chinese equivalent.

components.note: 见 (to see) — the act of looking.
又 (again, or a hand) — looking closely or repeatedly, giving 观 its meaning 'to observe, view.'
宀 (roof) — 察 relates to careful observation
祭 (jì) gives a loose sound connection to 察's reading chá

example.hanzi: 科学家仔细观察了这只昆虫的行为。
example.pinyin: Kēxuéjiā zǐxì guānchá le zhè zhī kūnchóng de xíngwéi.
example.english: The scientist carefully observed the insect's behavior.
example.fact: 观察 combines two verbs that both independently mean "to look, to watch" — 观 (as in 观看, "to view") and 察 (as in 察觉, "to detect, perceive") — into a single word for sustained, careful watching, distinct from a brief glance.

components.note: 耂 (a person bent with age, with long hair) — depicts an elderly figure.
匕 (here representing a cane or walking stick) — combined with the bent figure above, 老 pictures an old person leaning on a cane.
鼠 pictures a mouse in profile, with paws on one side and a long tail trailing on the other, giving the character its meaning 'mouse, rat.'

example.hanzi: 厨房里有一只老鼠。
example.pinyin: Chúfáng lǐ yǒu yì zhī lǎoshǔ.
example.english: There's a mouse in the kitchen.
example.fact: The 老 in 老鼠 isn't literally "old" — here it works as a fossilized, near-meaningless prefix that attaches to certain animal and kinship nouns for a familiar, colloquial ring (also seen in 老虎, "tiger," and 老师, "teacher"), rather than describing the mouse's actual age.

components.note: 田 (field) — represents farmland.
力 (strength/effort) — someone strong enough to work the fields gave 男 its meaning 'male, man.'
又 (hand), shown twice and joined together — two hands clasped in friendship gave 友 its meaning 'friend.'

example.hanzi: 她带男友回家见父母。
example.pinyin: Tā dài nányǒu huí jiā jiàn fùmǔ.
example.english: She brought her boyfriend home to meet her parents.
example.fact: 男友 is a clipped, modern shorthand for the fuller 男朋友 ("boyfriend") — dropping 朋 much like English speakers sometimes shorten "boyfriend" to "bf" in texting, though 男友 is common enough in writing and speech to not read as especially casual.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 掉 relates to dropping something from the hand.
卓 (zhuó) reflects an older phonetic connection that has faded in the modern pronunciation diào.

example.hanzi: 睡觉前记得关掉电视。
example.pinyin: Shuìjiào qián jìde guāndiào diànshì.
example.english: Remember to turn off the TV before going to bed.
example.fact: 掉 attached after a verb often marks that something is removed or eliminated as a result — 关掉 ("switch off," literally "close away"), 扔掉 ("throw away"), 忘掉 ("forget," literally "forget away") — a common verb-complement pattern for actions that make something disappear or cease.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 吃 relates to eating, done with the mouth
乞 (qǐ) gives a sound close to 吃's reading chī
忄 (heart) — 惊 relates to an emotional reaction of shock or fright
京 (jīng) gives the sound — an exact match with 惊's reading jīng

example.hanzi: 听到这个消息,大家都很吃惊。
example.pinyin: Tīngdào zhège xiāoxi, dàjiā dōu hěn chījīng.
example.english: Hearing this news, everyone was very shocked.
example.fact: 吃惊 literally reads "to eat a shock" — 吃 here isn't about food but uses its broader sense of "to take in, to undergo" (also seen in 吃苦, "to endure hardship," literally "to eat bitterness"), a small family of idioms where 吃 marks experiencing something sudden or unpleasant rather than consuming it.

components.note: A drawing of a person standing with arms and legs spread wide — used to represent the idea of something being 'big' or 'great.'
木 (wood) — buildings were traditionally framed with wood.
娄 (lóu) gives the sound — an exact match with 楼.

example.hanzi: 这座大楼有三十层。
example.pinyin: Zhè zuò dàlóu yǒu sānshí céng.
example.english: This building has thirty floors.
example.fact: 楼 alone already names a multistory building or a single floor within one (二楼, "the second floor") — 大楼 simply adds 大 ("big") to specify a sizeable one, typically an office or apartment tower, as distinct from a small standalone house (房子).

components.note: 力 (strength/force) — 动 relates to movement produced by exertion or force.

example.hanzi: 请不要移动这张桌子。
example.pinyin: Qǐng bú yào yídòng zhè zhāng zhuōzi.
example.english: Please don't move this table.
example.fact: 移动 has picked up a specialized modern sense as an adjective, "mobile" (移动电话, "mobile/cell phone"; 中国移动, "China Mobile," a major carrier) — an old, generic verb for physical movement of any kind repurposed to describe untethered, portable technology.

components.note: 冏 (bright, a window admitting light) — appears in 商's ancient form, though its exact link to 'commerce, to discuss' is unclear today.
章 — a graphic element whose original contribution to the character's meaning has been lost over time.
广 (shelter/building) — 店 names a building used for business.
占 (zhàn) gives a sound distantly related to diàn, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 这家商店周末不营业。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiā shāngdiàn zhōumò bù yíngyè.
example.english: This store isn't open on weekends.
example.fact: 商 alone already means "commerce, trade" (as in 商人, "merchant," and 商业, "business"), and 店 names the physical premises (as in 饭店, "restaurant/hotel") — 商店 simply combines "commerce" with "premises" into the generic word for any retail shop.

components.note: 女 depicts a kneeling woman.
支 depicts a hand holding a branch, suggesting work or a trade — paired with 女, it originally marked a woman working as an entertainer, giving 妓 its meaning 'prostitute.'
女 depicts a kneeling figure with arms crossed, a traditional posture — a simple picture of a woman.

example.hanzi: 这部电影描写了一个妓女的悲惨生活。
example.pinyin: Zhè bù diànyǐng miáoxiě le yí gè jìnǚ de bēicǎn shēnghuó.
example.english: This film depicts the tragic life of a prostitute.
example.fact: 妓 pairs 女 ("woman") with 支, which pictures a hand holding a branch and by extension "a trade, a skill" — together suggesting a woman working in an entertainment trade, the historical sense from which the character's narrower modern meaning developed.

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
斤 (an axe) — cutting through something.
米 (grain, in the simplified form; a bundle of thread in the traditional 斷) — the material being cut, giving 断 its meaning 'to break off, cut, sever.'

example.hanzi: 他不断地练习,直到学会为止。
example.pinyin: Tā bùduàn de liànxí, zhídào xuéhuì wéizhǐ.
example.english: He practiced continuously until he learned it.
example.fact: 断 alone means "to break, to sever" (as in 打断, "to interrupt," literally "to hit-break"), so 不断 literally reads "not broken" — describing an action or process as unbroken and continuous, the same negated-verb logic behind 不停 ("non-stop," literally "not stopping").

components.note: Originally a drawing of a bear, with 厶 as its head, ⺼ as its body, and 匕匕 as its claws; the picture was later borrowed to mean 'ability, to be able to.'
里 (a unit of distance, related to a village measure) — 量 relates to measuring quantity.
旦 (dàn) gives a hint of the sound — 量 is pronounced liàng, a connection that has shifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 运动可以释放身体里多余的能量。
example.pinyin: Yùndòng kěyǐ shìfàng shēntǐ lǐ duōyú de néngliàng.
example.english: Exercise can release the excess energy in the body.
example.fact: 能量 is a modern scientific coinage combining 能 ("ability, to be able") with 量 ("quantity, amount") into a literal "quantity of ability [to do work]" — a fairly transparent, compositional rendering of the physics concept "energy" built from two everyday characters rather than borrowed by sound.

components.note: 灬 (fire) — 熟 describes food that has been cooked thoroughly over fire.
孰 (shú) gives the sound — an exact match with 熟's reading shú.
心 (mind) — 悉 describes coming to fully know or understand something in one's mind.
釆 (biàn) is only distantly related in sound to xī — the connection has drifted apart to the point of being barely recognizable.

example.hanzi: 我对这座城市非常熟悉。
example.pinyin: Wǒ duì zhè zuò chéngshì fēicháng shúxī.
example.english: I'm very familiar with this city.
example.fact: 熟 alone already describes food that's fully cooked (成熟, "ripe, mature," shares the same root) — its extended sense "familiar, practiced" treats knowledge as something "cooked through," the same metaphor English uses when calling a skilled person "well-seasoned."

components.note: 八 here depicts something splitting apart or being divided.
厶 is an old form meaning 'private' or 'one's own' — 公 shows dividing up private property to share it fairly, giving rise to the meaning 'public' or 'fair.'
丶 (a dot) — represents the burning flame atop a lamp.
王 here depicts the base and stand of an oil lamp, not its usual meaning 'king' — the one who tends the flame became linked to 'master, lord, main.'

example.hanzi: 这个故事讲的是一位公主的冒险。
example.pinyin: Zhège gùshi jiǎng de shì yí wèi gōngzhǔ de màoxiǎn.
example.english: This story is about a princess's adventure.
example.fact: 公主's title is traditionally said to trace back to a Han-dynasty custom in which a duke (公) formally stood in as marriage sponsor for an emperor's daughter, since the emperor's own rank was considered too exalted for the role — hence "the one presented by a duke." Historians debate the details, but the 公 in the title is widely linked to this practice.

components.note: 月 (yuè) here actually derives from 肉 (meat) — 有 originally depicted a hand holding meat, meaning 'to possess'; it also lends a loose phonetic connection to yǒu.
攵 (an action/to strike) — 效 relates to the result produced by an action
交 (jiāo) gives a sound close to 效's reading xiào

example.hanzi: 这种方法非常有效。
example.pinyin: Zhè zhǒng fāngfǎ fēicháng yǒuxiào.
example.english: This method is very effective.
example.fact: 有效 literally combines 有 ("to have") with 效 ("effect, result") into "having effect" — the same 效 root appears in 效果 ("effect, result") and 有效期 ("period of validity"), the phrase commonly printed on medicine and food packaging as an expiration date.

components.note: 羊 (sheep; here representing feathers or ornaments on a headdress) — an elaborate decoration worn on the head.
大 (a person, arms outstretched) — a person wearing a decorated headdress was seen as beautiful, giving 美 its meaning 'beautiful.'
金 depicts a bell or metal casting mold, with dots representing droplets of molten metal — a picture linked to metal and, later, specifically gold.

example.hanzi: 这件衣服要一百美金。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn yīfu yào yìbǎi měijīn.
example.english: This piece of clothing costs one hundred US dollars.
example.fact: 美金 literally reads "American gold" — 金 here doesn't mean the metal but is a long-standing shorthand for "currency, money" (also seen in 现金, "cash") — distinct from the more official 美元, which uses 元, the standard word for a basic currency unit shared with 日元 ("yen") and 欧元 ("euro").

components.note: 夕 (evening/night) — the darkness that has fallen
亻 (a person) — someone moving under cover of night
日 (sun) — the sun is what disappears as evening falls
免 (to escape, avoid) — pictured as the sun slipping away, giving 晚 its sense of 'late, evening'

example.hanzi: 夜晚的城市非常安静。
example.pinyin: Yèwǎn de chéngshì fēicháng ānjìng.
example.english: The city is very quiet at night.
example.fact: 夜晚 doubles up two characters that both independently mean roughly "night, evening" — 夜 (built from 夕, "dusk," plus a person moving under cover of darkness) and 晚 (the sun "escaping," 免, out of sight) — reinforcing one meaning into a single, slightly more literary word for "nighttime."

components.note: 氵 (water) — relates to 清's meaning 'clear (water), pure.'
青 (qīng) gives the sound — 清 is also pronounced qīng, an exact match.
酉 (wine jar) — 醒 originally described sobering up from drink, extending to 'to wake up.'
星 (xīng) gives a sound close to xǐng, sharing the same syllable body and differing mainly in tone.

example.hanzi: 喝了咖啡后,他感觉更清醒了。
example.pinyin: Hē le kāfēi hòu, tā gǎnjué gèng qīngxǐng le.
example.english: After drinking coffee, he felt more clear-headed.
example.fact: 醒 (built from 酉, "wine jar") originally described sobering up from drink before broadening into the general sense "to wake up" — so 清醒 literally combines "clear" with "sobered-up," letting the word cover both waking from literal sleep and having a clear, alert mind more generally.
